newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Southern Africa air cargo rise beats world average.
newsitem.headline: Southern Africa air cargo rise beats world average.

text.p: Southern African air cargo business surged last year with the cargo industry reporting growth of up to 48 percent in volume, easily beating the global average, airlines said this week.
The Boeing Company forecast in June 1996 that world air cargo traffic would grow at 6.7 percent a year until 2015.
Swissair Cargo experienced the most growth with a 48 percent increase in imports to Cape Town and exports up 25 percent. In Johannesburg imports were up 17 percent and exports up 25 percent.
"We have had quiet good growth. We added one flight and now have five flights operating in southern Africa," Swissair sales manager Nancy Pronto told Reuters.
British Airways World Cargo experienced a 40 percent increase in volumes to 4,700 kg between April and November 1996 compared to the previous period.

The service delivery manager Africa, Richard Poulton, said growth was largely due to the establishment of a dedicated cargo centre in Johannesburg and increasing the number of flights to southern Africa.
He said they expected similar growth in 1997.
South African Airways Cargoc expected a 26.5 percent increase in tonnage handled in the 1996/97 period from a 36.4 percent increase in 1995/96. Its year ends in March.
It operates five dedicated freighter aircrafts besides the belly of passenger planes.
Lufthansa Cargo said it experienced a slight drop in exports to 10,374 tons in 1996 from 11,826 tons in 1995, but anticipated steady growth of 15 percent to continue over the next few years.

"The decline in the export side is mainly due to capacity releases to Nairobi due to higher yields and the good perishable season, as well as the two direct flights to Namibia," Lufthansa Cargo sales and marketing manager Bettina Faulhaber said.
Imports grew to 10,300 tons in 1996 from 10,150 in 1995, she said.

SAA Cargo general manager Charles Fairweather said jet fuel prices had increased by up to 49 percent but the fuel price hikes might not be passed on fully to customers due to high competition in the industry.

"Due to extreme competition it is unlikely that price increases of such magnitude will be passed on to the consumer. However, it can only mean that the industry is in for a period of rationalisation," Fairweather said.

The airlines said the most frequently imported goods included machinery, manufactured goods, electronics and cars. The most frequently exported goods included fruits and vegetables, flowers, car accessories, precious metals and live animals.
The most favoured export destinations are Europe and the Middle East, they said.
SAA Cargo said the faltering rand, which lost 29 percent of its value against the U.S. dollar in 1996, was putting pressure on South African imports and favouring exports.
Exports handled by SAA Cargo from January to July 1996 grew by 17.8 percent compared to a 12.3 percent rise in the same period in 1995.
Imports grew by 15.5 percent in January to July of 1996 compared to a 29.2 percent in the same period in 1995.
Pronto said South African exporters were less experienced to compete in the export market.
"We need more experience for (South African) exporters in overseas markets to be more competitive," she said.
